Support comes in two kinds: direct support (patterns we are "entitled to expect" if h is true) and indirect support (patterns incompatible with relevant alternatives). Where to stop probing is set by context, meaning background knowledge, a default entitlement to other scientists' claims, and cost-benefit values. | [LIT-139](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-139.md) v2 | Inductive Risk and Values in Science | Douglas (2000), DOI-10.1086/392855. Hempel's "inductive risk" (the chance of wrongly accepting or rejecting a hypothesis) arises at three internal stages of science: choosing a methodology such as a significance level, characterising data, and interpreting results. Wherever the non-epistemic consequences of error can be foreseen, weighing them requires non-epistemic values. Douglas shows this on dioxin cancer studies. Three pathologist panels (1978, 1980, 1990) scored the same Kociba rat-liver slides differently (e.g. 34/50, 33/47, 18/50 tumours at 100 ng/kg/day). Choosing between threshold and no-threshold readings of the same data has meant regulatory limits about 100× apart. Values enter only indirectly, through the consequences of error, never as evidence that a claim is true. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-145](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-145.md)); worth reading as the canonical, compact statement of the modern inductive-risk argument. It is carefully scoped, with an explicit direct/indirect distinction and exemptions for negligible uncertainty and consequence-free research, and it is well illustrated. Its normative premise, that scientists bear moral responsibility for foreseeable consequences of error, is explicitly left unargued (§2, p. 563). |

| [LIT-161](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-161.md) v2 | Why Replication Is Overrated | Feest (2019), DOI-10.1086/705451. Every experiment and every replication rests on individuation judgments about what is being manipulated and measured ("conceptual scope"). So direct replication can at most help rule out random error, and "perhaps" establish that some effect exists but not which effect, while conceptual replication begs the question by presupposing that two operationalisations individuate the same effect. | [LIT-175](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-175.md) v2 | Evidence in Medicine and Evidence-Based Medicine | Worrall (2007), DOI-10.1111/j.1747-9991.2007.00106.x. Worrall argues that the EBM evidence hierarchy has no sound general rationale for giving randomisation extra epistemic weight, even though it lets high-quality RCTs "trump any number of observational studies". He examines five standard arguments. Four fail: (a) Fisher's significance-test logic, (b) control of unknown confounders, (d) that observational studies "exaggerate" effects, and (e) probabilistic causality. The fifth, (c) selection bias, is a "cast-iron argument", but it supports only taking allocation out of the clinicians' hands, and randomisation is one way to do that. What matters is balance on plausible confounders, a placebo or active control and blinding. Whether balance comes from randomising or from matching "seems epistemically unimportant", and historically controlled trials can give strong evidence for large effects. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-126](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-126.md)); worth reading as the fullest single statement of the philosophical case against the special epistemic standing of randomisation. | [LIT-187](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-187.md) v3 | On the Philosophy of Unsupervised Learning | Watson (2023), DOI-10.1007/s13347-023-00635-6. Watson argues that clustering, abstraction and generative modelling each come with an epistemic thesis (EC, EA, EG — we identify natural kinds, essential properties and unrealized possibilities via such algorithms or something like them), which he accepts. Each also comes with an ontological thesis (OC, OA, OG — these just *are* what the algorithms ought to find under ideal conditions), which he rejects because nothing guarantees they are effectively computable. He adds a pragmatic, context-relative view of natural kinds, and closes with the claim that unsupervised outputs are neither "objective" nor vacuous. They should be validated by error-statistical means: resampling stability, generalization of clusters to held-out data, out-of-sample likelihood, and train-on-synthetic scores. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-172](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-172.md)); worth reading as the most systematic philosophical treatment of unsupervised learning as a family, and as the target of Søgaard's reply. Its headline claims ("perhaps the most fundamental branch of all AI") are argued more thinly than its E/O structure. |

Leonelli argues that mainstream, institutional Open Science treats openness as the unlimited, digital sharing of research objects, a transparency-first ordering running transparency → quality (reproducibility) → inclusion. This rests on an object-oriented, "resourcist" epistemology of science. Four implementation cases (GISAID COVID data, open-source software stigma, crop-data linkage, the reproducibility "crisis") show it can narrow epistemic diversity and entrench epistemic injustice, which lowers reliability. | [LIT-213](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-213.md) v2 | Rigour versus the need for evidential diversity | Cartwright (2021), DOI-10.1007/s11229-021-03368-1. Cartwright offers a characterisation of "rigour": a method is rigorous when a valid argument shows its results are evidence for the conclusion and its premises are well established or secured by design. On that definition even well-run RCTs often fail to rigorously establish a study-population ATE, because orthogonality holds only at assignment and the potential-outcomes premise carries heavy metaphysics, and they seldom answer singular questions. Her alternative is a causal-process-tracing theory of change (pToC) with five elements (steps, causal principles, support factors, derailers, safeguards). It catalogues the diverse and mostly non-rigorous evidence that singular causal predictions need. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-161](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-161.md)); worth reading as a compact, citable statement of the "rigour is overvalued, evidence the causal process" position. | [LIT-216](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-216.md) v2 | The Weirdness of the World | Schwitzgebel (2024), DOI-10.1515/9780691239309. The book's thesis is that every viable theory of how consciousness fits into the cosmos, and of the cosmos's basic structure, is both "bizarre" (contrary to common sense) and "dubious" (not rationally compelling). So "something that seems almost too crazy to believe must be true" (p. 4), and credence should be spread across the bizarre options. Examples of those options are that the United States is conscious (if materialism is true), that we are sims or Boltzmann brains (a 0.1–1% credence), that space is transcendentally ideal, that almost every act causes almost every future event, and that there is no fact about snail consciousness. Its only positive empirical results are three self-experiments against solipsism (for example, 17 of 19 decisive chess games lost, p < .001). "Can machines think?" is replaced by whether a digital computer can play the imitation game so that an interrogator, questioning by teleprinter, identifies it no more reliably than he tells a man from a woman. Universality reduces the question to one computer suitably programmed. Turing predicts that by about 2000 a machine with 10^9 bits of storage will leave an average interrogator no more than a 70 per cent chance of a right identification after five minutes. He answers nine objections, the argument from consciousness by its collapse into solipsism, and proposes reaching the goal by educating a child-machine. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-355](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-355.md)); worth reading as the source of the imitation game and as the first catalogue of objections to machine thought, nine of them, each still argued. Read it for what it actually proposes: not a definition of thinking but the replacement of an ill-posed question by a test, a prediction about 2000 (70 per cent right identification after five minutes, at 10^9 bits), and a programme for reaching it by educating a child-machine. Its reply to the argument from consciousness is an other-minds argument, not a theory of consciousness, and Turing says outright that he does not think there is "no mystery about consciousness". |

It turns the 1971 paper's observer-relativity ([LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md)) into "the facts about the success or failure of the stance … are perfectly objective", introduces the Martian thought experiment and the intentional "real patterns" later worked out in [LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md), and runs the thermostat-to-person continuum ("no magic moment"). Its criterion admits any system on which the strategy pays, groups included, but the essay never applies it to a group. |
| [LIT-411](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-411.md) | Could a Large Language Model be Conscious? | Chalmers (2023), arXiv:2303.07103; Boston Review, 9 August 2023; from a NeurIPS 2022 invited talk. Asks for a feature X that LLMs have (or lack) and that indicates consciousness (or its absence). Self-report, seeming-conscious, conversation and general intelligence give at most weak evidence for it. Biology, senses and embodiment, world and self models, recurrent processing, a global workspace and unified agency are the evidence against. All but biology are temporary. On mainstream assumptions: under 10% credence for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade. Twelve challenges are offered as roadmap or red flags. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-345.md)), from arXiv v3 (the Boston Review text), with v1's conclusions compared; worth reading as the clearest short statement of the case for and against consciousness in LLMs, and as the origin of the "theory-balanced" credence approach that Butlin et al. built on. Its method is a regimented request for a feature X, and its verdicts are credences offered "for illustrative purposes": under 10% for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade, on "mainstream assumptions". It does not break the deadlock [THEORY-023](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-023.md) describes. It is an instance of it: mimicry undercuts self-report, the main obstacles are theory-derived, and biology is set aside rather than answered. |
| [LIT-421](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-421.md) | Foreword | Chalmers (2008), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195333213.002.0007. The co-author's retrospective on the extended mind: his iPhone is "part of my mind already". The one principled objection is that perception and action bound the mental. His reply is revisionist and contextualist: whether Otto's belief counts as extended flips with explanatory purpose. No Otto-style twin case works for consciousness, so he tentatively keeps an internal conscious core. The thesis needs only a weak, parity-style functionalism and is compatible with dualism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-369](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-369.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of where Chalmers stands on the thesis he co-authored, ten years on. Three things in eight pages: the iPhone as a present-day Otto's notebook; the perception-action boundary as the one principled objection, answered by explanatory revisionism and a "Necker cube" view on which whether Otto's belief is extended depends on explanatory purpose; and a tentative internal "conscious core", resting on the failure of any Otto-style twin case for consciousness. It is a foreword: every position is stated briefly and several are offered as "perhaps". |
| [LIT-425](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-425.md) | The Meta-Problem of Consciousness | Chalmers (2018), Journal of Consciousness Studies 25(9–10):6–61. The meta-problem is to explain, in terms that do not mention consciousness, why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem. It is an "easy" problem with an empirical programme. Of thirteen candidate mechanisms, the most promising is an introspective model that attributes primitive relations of awareness to primitive qualities, with a sense of acquaintance. A realist theory should explain how its basis of consciousness produces these judgments, which IIT and biological theories struggle to do. Debunking arguments for illusionism can be blocked, but a residual sense of coincidence remains. Only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, and it is false because people feel pain. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-354](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-354.md)); worth reading as the statement of the meta-problem, explaining in topic-neutral terms why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem, and as a survey of thirteen candidate mechanisms. Cite it for four things: the meta-problem as an "easy" problem with a research programme; the meta-problem challenge to theories of consciousness, which tells against IIT and biological theories; the analysis of debunking and coincidence arguments for illusionism; and the argument that only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, with a Moorean rejection of strong illusionism. Its own preferred solution is offered as "closer to a fleshed-out explanandum" than an explanation. |
| [LIT-430](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-430.md) | The Intentional Stance | Dennett (1987), MIT Press. Per its publisher, the "first full-scale presentation of a theory of intentionality" Dennett had been developing for almost twenty years: we understand each other by adopting a stance, "a predictive strategy of interpretation that presupposes the rationality" of whatever we predict. Six chapters reprint papers of the 1980s, each followed by a new "Reflections" essay; the first and the last three chapters are new. Chapter 2 is True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)). Unread: registered from the description and a catalogue's contents note. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and a library catalogue's contents note, not read: no lawful full text of the book could be reached. The Internet Archive scans are lending-only (access-restricted, printdisabled), the MIT Press page and loc.gov were blocked, and the Tufts Digital Library holds earlier versions of several chapters as papers but not the book. Its chapter 2 is True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)), read in full in its 1997 reprint, which is the revised book text. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-433](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-433.md) | Quining Qualia | Dennett (1988), in Marcel & Bisiach (eds.), Consciousness in Contemporary Science, OUP, pp. 42–77. Qualia as tradition has them are ineffable, intrinsic, private and directly apprehensible, and fifteen intuition pumps argue that nothing has all four. Two neurosurgical routes to an apparent colour inversion, one changing qualia and one only memory-linked reactions, feel the same from the inside. So the subject cannot know his own qualia better than an outside tester can. What is real is practical ineffability and idiosyncrasy: we refer to information-rich public properties through our own detectors of them. Hence "there simply are no qualia at all". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-357](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-357.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of qualia eliminativism and the source of the post-Cartesian side in the record's consciousness readings. It argues by fifteen intuition pumps, not by proof, and says so. Its lasting results are two: the alternative-neurosurgery and Chase-and-Sanborn cases, which show that neither the subject nor the physiologist can separate a change in qualia from a change in reactions to them; and a positive account of practical ineffability and privacy as idiosyncratic, information-rich property detection. Its conclusion, "there simply are no qualia at all", is a tactical choice of words by the author's own endnote 2, not a stronger thesis than that. |
| [LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md) | Intentional Systems | Dennett (1971), Journal of Philosophy 68(4):87–106. An Intentional system is one whose behaviour can be explained and predicted by ascribing beliefs and desires and assuming rationality, which is the Intentional stance beside the design and physical stances. Being one is relative to an observer's strategy, and the choice of stance is pragmatic. The stance is "unmetaphysical": it sets aside composition, consciousness and moral standing. As psychology it is vacuous, because it presupposes rationality. Any theory that gives content to a part takes out a "loan of intelligence", repayable only by analysing away the part's reader: "there a little man is concealed". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-350](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-350.md)); worth reading as the first statement in print of the intentional stance and of the homunculus debt that Dennett later answers with "discharge". Its definition makes being an Intentional system relative to an observer's predictive strategy, and it says outright that the definition "does not say that Intentional systems really have beliefs and desires" (p. 91). True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)) later withdraws exactly that relativity. Its lasting tool for this record is the "loan of intelligence" (p. 96): any theory that gives a part content owes an account of that part's reader, and "wherever a theory relies on a formulation bearing the logical marks of Intentionality, there a little man is concealed". The paper does not treat a group as an Intentional system. |
| [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md) | Of Personal Identity | Hume (1739), Treatise 1.4.6, with the Appendix (1740). There is no impression of a self, "constant and invariable", so no idea of one: introspection finds only "some particular perception or other", and the mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". The identity we ascribe to it is "fictitious", like that of plants, ships and churches: an easy transition of the imagination along resemblance and causation, with memory discovering rather than producing it, so that hard cases are "grammatical" rather than philosophical. The Appendix retracts the account of the connecting principle: two principles he cannot reconcile or renounce leave the matter "too hard for my understanding". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md)), in the Merivale–Millican critical text on davidhume.org, with the Appendix's second thoughts (App. 10–21); worth reading as the founding statement of the bundle view and the first published retraction of it. The section finds no impression of a self, calls the mind "a bundle or collection of different perceptions", and explains our ascription of identity to it as a fiction of the imagination run on resemblance and causation, the same fiction that makes a repaired ship or a rebuilt church "the same". The Appendix then confesses that it cannot explain what unites the perceptions and leaves the problem "too hard for my understanding". The section's case is introspective and associationist; its Appendix is the clearest statement of what any bundle view owes. |
| [LIT-458](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-458.md) | Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness | Frankish (2016), Journal of Consciousness Studies 23(11–12):11–39, the target article of the issue later published as Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness (2017). Names "illusionism": phenomenal properties are not instantiated, and the task is the "illusion problem" of explaining why experiences seem to have them. Strong illusionism (no phenomenal properties at all, only "quasi-phenomenal" physical ones introspection misrepresents) is separated from weak illusionism (real phenomenal properties that merely seem ineffable, intrinsic, private), which it argues collapses into the strong form or into radical realism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-384](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-384.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of illusionism under that name, and the target article that Dennett's "Illusionism as the Obvious Default Theory of Consciousness" ([LIT-434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-434.md)) answers. It names the "illusion problem", draws the strong/weak illusionism line with "quasi-phenomenal" properties, and argues from conservatism, anomalousness and the debunking argument that strong illusionism should be the research programme. It states a programme, not a theory: by its own account it "will not propose a detailed illusionist theory" (p. 1 of the eprint), and its positive arguments are abductive and openly so. |
| [LIT-470](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-470.md) | Foundations for a Social Ontology | Thomasson (2003), ProtoSociology 18–19:269–290. Per its abstract: the social world poses a metaphysical puzzle (how facts and objects created by human intentionality can be real) and an epistemological one (how such products can include objective facts for the social sciences to discover). Searle's account in The Construction of Social Reality is too narrow to solve either; rules for constructing social reality that parallel rules for make-believe give a more comprehensive ontology, but talk of social reality is not pretence. Unread: filed from the abstract. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's abstract; no lawful full text was reachable (the Philosophy Documentation Center sells it at $20, PhilPapers returned 403, and the Academia.edu copy sits behind a bot check), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. By its abstract it argues that Searle's account of social facts is too narrow and that rules modelled on the rules of make-believe give a fuller social ontology; how, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-474](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-474.md) | The Social Construction of Reality: A Treatise in the Sociology of Knowledge | Berger & Luckmann (1966), Doubleday. A treatise in the sociology of knowledge. By its contents: the reality of everyday life and its language; society as objective reality (institutionalization, sedimentation and tradition, roles, legitimation, symbolic universes); society as subjective reality (primary and secondary socialization, identity). Unread: filed from catalogue records and the table of contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records and the 1966 edition's table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scans of the 1966 Doubleday edition and a 1967 printing are lending-only, and there is no author-posted text), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the sociology-of-knowledge treatise whose title phrase [ADR-017](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md)'s topic blurb uses; what it claims, beyond its contents page, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md) | The Construction of Social Reality | Searle (1995), Free Press, New York (xiii + 241 pp.). The founding book of Searle's social ontology. Per its catalogue description, it argues that some facts are independent of human observers and some require human agreement. Its chapters move from the building blocks of social reality and the creation of institutional facts through language and a general theory of institutional facts, to a defence of external realism and the correspondence theory of truth. Unread: filed from the catalogue record and contents; the record reads the theory in Searle's 2006 restatement. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from catalogue records and a library scan of the table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in print with Free Press / Simon & Schuster, the Internet Archive copies are either lending-only or unauthorised uploads, and Searle posted no draft), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. The record reads the theory through Searle's own 2006 restatement ([LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md), read in full), which is the entry to start from. |
| [LIT-492](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-492.md) | On Social Facts | Gilbert (1989), Routledge (reissued by Princeton University Press, 1992; DOI-10.1515/9780691214627). The book asks whether social groups are real over and above individuals' thoughts. It analyses everyday concepts of social action, social groups, collective belief and social convention, in dialogue with Weber, Simmel, Durkheim and David Lewis, and proposes that core social phenomena are "plural subject" phenomena. Unread: filed from the publishers' descriptions and the chapter list. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publishers' records and the chapter list; no lawful full text was reachable (the Princeton reissue is sold as an e-book on De Gruyter, and the Internet Archive's copy of the Routledge edition is lending-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is Gilbert's book-length treatment of plural subjects, collective belief and social convention; "Walking Together" ([LIT-477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-477.md)) is the short version. |
